title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of workers' daily life on film
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on photographing its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the ten-thousand-worker plant really did disappear, only a very few people had kept that archive.
why: This is not industry analysis; it is a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in the shift in manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show promo and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value not matter
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process so that manufacturing output is more stable and the people are more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean: anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. There were no machines replacing people yet, but a person's value already barely mattered. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system that deliberately erases individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like riding into a bandit's den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed the glass with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he could not sit and could not drink water; after getting off, his belly was terribly swollen. At the Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold as a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan and said it was for Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway toll, and if you refused someone would come up and slap you, and in the end they dumped you in a wasteland with no village ahead and no shop behind to change vehicles. He says he used the term for years and only understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was very hard to find work after coming out; men had a far harder time than women, and factory recruitment notices stated outright that they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began to drop, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was left. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar with someone; the other man flashed a split, he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, well, if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 a roll, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — in that era an enormous drain on him. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war, assuming instinctively that photography was just a matter of technique, of getting it sharp. Later he read Chinese photography magazines and found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard by which to measure it, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding model contests; the women went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms they had made, and there was pole dancing too. In 2008 he changed position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience in the distance — and sent it to Tencent in time; it went up on the portal and drew tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss, a lover for the factory director; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure and told him to delete it. Tencent said it could only be hidden, that other sites' viral re-posting could not be stopped, and finally served him a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he went into the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allows a four-minute break after two hours; the place where they changed work clothes was hung all over with clean-room suits nobody was wearing, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the lesson others taught him when learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he long avoided using this one. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he admitted it has its own pull — different readers will have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was separate, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system did not require contributions, so this set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system would not accept it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the enterprises decided you were dishonest and zeroed out your years of service. He says this will not do; our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those many years of service are real. When even present-day life is not secure, it is simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

points.h: Density: he shot for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the thread of dense migrant-worker life, which won an excellence award and the Alpa prize at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' assemblies shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung all over with clothes, from a distance airtight; and workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual sense of density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting with his phone every day, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many factories and so much of an era, he had not observed it that way; then one morning he found it so terrifying that even a switch looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as the warp, space as the weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out is: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, and capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a composite three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword dagong (working for wages), he looked up ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, got 322 of them, went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting all of them — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be presented together with his own understanding from actually shooting, in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us viewing the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers get the credit, but it is the Sherpas who carry the loads — I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it meant being cheated en route to work by brokers and drivers who piled on charges layer by layer.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
The internationally known photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers one by one on its website.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't about getting on a train — you felt you had climbed into a bandit's den.
This is the era: we view the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we reach will certainly not be poor; but if we can see a society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
